LightPath Technologies.why: Makes infrared and visible optical components, assemblies and modules, Black Diamond infrared glass used instead of germanium (melted in its own glass plants) and infrared cameras/seekers; demand for its optics, glass and assemblies drives its revenue directly (fiscal 2026 revenue up 93% to $71.7 million, backlog $110.9 million).
LightPath Technologies.evidence: LightPath Technologies Q4 FY2026 (09-10-2026): CEO Sam Rubin: 'As of this fall, LightPath now does everything - melts glass, coats optics, builds cameras and assemblies - exclusively outside of China in Orlando, in Plano, Texas, in Hudson, New Hampshire, and in Riga, Latvia'; CFO Albert Miranda: 'Sales of infrared components were $21.2 million ... Visible components were $15.5 million ... Assemblies and modules were $31.9 million'.

players.product: infrared and visible optical components, Black Diamond infrared glass (used instead of germanium), assemblies and modules, and infrared cameras

quarterly_data.signal: Fiscal Q4 2026 record quarter (CEO Sam Rubin, CFO Albert Miranda): revenue $21.2 million, up 73% from $12.2 million in the year-ago quarter - a company record and the fourth consecutive quarter of sequential growth. By product group: infrared components $7.1 million (34% of revenue), visible components $4.2 million (20%), assemblies and modules $9.1 million (43%), engineering services $800 thousand (4%). Gross profit rose 210% to $8.3 million, a 39.4% gross margin vs 22% a year earlier; adjusted EBITDA $2.1 million (10% of revenue) vs an adjusted EBITDA loss of $2.0 million, the fourth consecutive quarter of positive adjusted EBITDA; net loss $4.1 million ($0.06 per share) vs $7.1 million ($0.16 per share).
quarterly_data.figure: Q4 revenue $21.2 million (+73% YoY); gross margin 39.4% (22% a year earlier); adjusted EBITDA $2.1 million (10% of revenue); net loss $4.1 million

quarterly_data.signal: Fiscal 2026 full year (CFO Albert Miranda): revenue up 93% to $71.7 million from $37.2 million in fiscal 2025 - infrared components $21.2 million (30% of revenue, up 52%), visible components $15.5 million (22%, up 32%), assemblies and modules $31.9 million (44%, up 281%), engineering services $3.1 million (4%, roughly flat). Gross margin expanded from 27% to 36%; adjusted EBITDA was a $4.2 million profit vs a $5.1 million loss in fiscal 2025, a swing of $9.3 million. CEO Sam Rubin: assemblies, modules and cameras were 43% of Q4 and 44% of the full year vs 23% of revenue in fiscal 2025; the 39.4% Q4 margin 'did not come from a one-time favorable contract or from raising prices' but from that mix (higher prices and margins than the legacy component business) and from execution - past yield and throughput problems in components are 'in the past', and every one of the four product groups improved its margin year over year. CFO: the margin also reflected better absorption on higher volume and a $5 million inventory reserve charge in the prior year that did not recur. Year-end cash was $93.2 million with effectively no debt.
quarterly_data.figure: FY2026 revenue $71.7 million (+93% from $37.2 million); gross margin 36% (27% in FY2025); adjusted EBITDA $4.2 million (loss of $5.1 million in FY2025); cash $93.2 million

quarterly_data.signal: CFO Albert Miranda on costs: Q4 operating expenses were $12.6 million vs $7.2 million a year earlier; $2.0 million of the increase was a noncash fair-value adjustment to acquisition earn-out liabilities, primarily G5 Infrared reflecting its strong performance against the earn-out targets, and the remaining $3.4 million was mainly SG&A (the addition of AMI operations, incentive compensation accruals, senior leadership additions, higher sales and marketing, IT spend to meet customer security requirements). Fiscal 2026 operating expenses were $45.5 million vs $22.0 million, including $14.1 million of noncash earn-out fair-value adjustment; new product development costs also increased. The $15.6 million fiscal 2026 earn-out charge remeasures what the G5 sellers earned because G5 is outperforming the estimate made at acquisition; the final G5 earn-out was agreed and accrued in Q4 for payment in January 2027, with possible small future adjustments related to AMI and Visimid.
quarterly_data.figure: Q4 opex $12.6 million (incl. $2.0 million earn-out adjustment); FY2026 opex $45.5 million (incl. $14.1 million earn-out adjustment); FY2026 earn-out charge $15.6 million

quarterly_data.signal: Backlog at June 30 was $110.9 million, up 197% from $37.4 million a year earlier, with approximately $85.6 million requested by customers for delivery within 12 months (CFO Albert Miranda). CEO Sam Rubin: backlog did not grow sequentially in Q4, but shortly after quarter-end the company reported two large orders totaling $24 million (July) and has kept booking, so the next quarter's backlog will already show more growth. The two July orders are for 2027 delivery, already in production and on a cadence of deliveries spread over months, and are expected to be renewed in the years to come as programs of record typically are; much of the current ordering is for production as programs move from qualification to production. By application, counter-UAS is 'still probably one of the biggest parts of the backlog', optics for drones and assemblies for drone dominance are a growing part, and there is not a lot of border patrol in it yet.
quarterly_data.figure: Backlog $110.9 million (+197% from $37.4 million); ~$85.6 million for delivery within 12 months; two July orders totaling $24 million

quarterly_data.signal: CEO Sam Rubin: capacity is the single biggest operational theme for fiscal 2027 and glass is 'by far' the biggest capacity constraint - demand for glass is running ahead of supply even after the January acquisition of Amorphous Materials (AMI), which increased BlackDiamond melting capacity and unlocked large-diameter melting up to 10 inches and beyond vs the 5 inches produced before (large diameter opens long-range camera systems, large assemblies and space-based missile detection and tracking); doubling glass capacity was 'nowhere near enough'. LightPath is adding melting capacity in Orlando and Texas (and will probably need even more), moving AMI's operations into a larger building near its Visimid camera business in the Dallas area, and expanding optical fabrication, coating and assembly across its U.S. and Latvian sites, adding shifts in all locations. After glass, detectors are the long pole: lead times have grown from about six months to ten months or more, so the company is building inventory ahead; mechanics, motors (magnets) and other components have also become material constraints.
quarterly_data.figure: Large-diameter glass melting up to 10 inches (vs 5 inches before); detector lead times from about six months to ten months or more

quarterly_data.signal: Capex was $6.3 million in fiscal 2026, $4.4 million of it in Q4 - the last time LightPath spent at that level was calendar 2023, when it expanded the Orlando facility and doubled the clean room (CFO Albert Miranda). Fiscal 2027 capex will be higher than fiscal 2026, 'a deliberate choice made against a visible order book and pipeline' (CEO Sam Rubin): all locations will be expanded to meet the backlog and the demand foreseen through fiscal 2027 and into fiscal 2028, getting ahead of demand in key areas like BlackDiamond glass production. CEO on fiscal 2027: 'less about proving the thesis and more about scaling against it. Doubling a manufacturing business in 12 months is hard. Doing it twice in a row is harder, and it will require capacity we are still building and people we are still hiring.' CFO: the fiscal 2027 mandate is to add capacity fast enough, hold the margin gains and convert the book, and it is 'fully funded'. CEO: the company will also pursue accretive, capability-adding acquisitions similar to G5 and AMI.
quarterly_data.figure: FY2026 capex $6.3 million ($4.4 million in Q4); FY2027 capex to be higher than FY2026

quarterly_data.signal: CEO Sam Rubin on germanium substitution: China's first restrictions on germanium and gallium exports in late 2024 started a growth in demand for BlackDiamond glass and systems using it; redesigns to BlackDiamond and new programs - whose design and qualification can take up to two years - are now beginning to move into production, and much of the recent backlog and bookings growth comes from them. He expects the trend to intensify because most customers did not start their redesign and substitution effort until well after the initial germanium export ban; new customers are being won both by converting them to BlackDiamond and by supplying assemblies and systems. LightPath has two domestic glass plants and, in his words, 'the broadest portfolio of infrared materials available'. On germanium supply he now sees more runway than he first thought: one of the leading companies noted current production of only three to four tons per year with increases several years out, and U.S. mining or refining awards also talk about single-digit tons, so new capacity will not solve the problem in the near term.
quarterly_data.figure: Design and qualification up to two years; germanium production of only three to four tons per year at one of the leading companies

quarterly_data.signal: China exit (CEO Sam Rubin): in July LightPath signed a definitive agreement to sell its China subsidiary to an entity owned by the local management team that ran the facility, expected to close 'later this month'. Roughly $1.5 million of annual third-party revenue leaves the consolidated results; the entity will keep supplying LightPath as a third-party vendor for its commercial customers in the U.S. and Europe, so there is no disruption to them. LightPath now melts glass, coats optics and builds cameras and assemblies exclusively outside China - in Orlando, Plano (Texas), Hudson (New Hampshire) and Riga (Latvia) - with no ownership, facility or commercial activity in China; six years ago most of its manufacturing was in China and more than a third of revenue came from China. CEO: for a customer base now dominated by defense primes and public safety agencies, this opens significant bid opportunities where it is a condition for participation. Defense programs must move optical glass and optical component sourcing from covered nations before the end of the decade; with two-to-three-year qualification cycles, the sourcing decisions for 2029 and 2030 are being made now, and executive orders on germanium waivers, critical-material classification and tariffs would likely pull the timeline closer.
quarterly_data.figure: Roughly $1.5 million of annual third-party revenue leaves with the China subsidiary

quarterly_data.signal: NGSRI, LightPath's three-year-old interceptor program with Lockheed Martin (CEO Sam Rubin): the Army has pushed out the timeline by a few months to potentially explore other options; he sees a delay, not a risk - the new missiles must be reverse-compatible with the tens of thousands of fielded Stinger launchers, primes such as Lockheed and Raytheon have worked on it for three years, and it is 'highly unlikely' that someone else has an equally mature solution in a short time frame. The full qualification of LightPath's low-cost seeker, completed as a result of the NGSRI flight test, opens the door to other opportunities: its camera systems are now designed into or actively evaluated in seven different platforms, three of them with Lockheed Martin and the rest with primes or newer defense entrants ('neoprimes'), all supported from the same Texas manufacturing facility. The seeker groups were relocated into a new building and LightPath has begun investing in seeker-building capacity so a program moving into production can scale quickly. CEO: there is a big push to refill inventories of interceptors like THAAD and Patriot PAC-3 and likely a bigger push for next-generation interceptors; LightPath is involved in many interceptor and precision-munition types but gave no specific numbers.
quarterly_data.figure: Camera systems designed into or evaluated in seven platforms, three with Lockheed Martin

quarterly_data.signal: CEO Sam Rubin on other defense programs: in border tower programs DHS has released funding to the prime, but it has not yet turned into camera orders; demand is growing instead for similar towers and cameras installed outside the U.S., primarily in the Middle East - mostly foreign military sales to allies for border towers in Middle East or North African countries, where LightPath is typically one step down with subprimes and each deal is usually 'in the tens of millions of dollars' for it. Air Force and Army opportunities are mainly counter-UAS and ISR systems. An unnamed airborne program has completed qualification and awaits the LRIP production order; the Apache program may make a comeback with renewed interest. Drone and drone-dominance programs are generating significant demand, which LightPath is meeting by adding automation for high-volume assemblies; two counter-UAS programs are transitioning to a cadence of deliveries of tens of systems a month. SPEIR cameras for the Navy: the first camera, or maybe two, have shipped and another five are in dispatch, expected to ship in the next few weeks.
quarterly_data.figure: Border tower deals usually tens of millions of dollars each; counter-UAS deliveries of tens of systems a month; five more SPEIR cameras in dispatch

quarterly_data.signal: New products, all using BlackDiamond glass instead of germanium (CEO Sam Rubin): the redesign of the last G5 cooled cameras with BlackDiamond is progressing well technically but is behind schedule, and results so far indicate the cameras will work at least as well as the germanium-based ones; the delay reflects stretched supply chains (especially detectors, plus mechanics, other lenses and component changes) and Amorphous melting that glass at that size at scale for one of the first times, which needs fine-tuning. In long-wave infrared (uncooled) cameras, a year-long effort on zoom lenses and zoom cameras is coming to fruition, with the first orders for zoom lenses and complete uncooled zoom cameras to be delivered soon; once fully production-ready he expects market need to translate into orders fairly quickly.
